query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing ~5 at.% Al into a CoFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy and annealing to induce partial B2-phase ordering will increase domain-wall pinning and magnetocrystalline anisotropy, thereby raising the coercive field at room temperature compared to an Al-free baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic CoFeMnNi alloy arc-melted and homogenized under vacuum without Al addition.
generation.intervention: Add ~5 at.% Al and perform vacuum annealing at ~800 °C for 12–24 hours to promote partial B2-type ordering.
generation.conditions: Arc-melt both doped and undoped alloys, homogenize, vacuum anneal at ~800 °C, and cool to room temperature before magnetic measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered B2-phase domains in the CoFeMnNi(Al) matrix.
generation.mechanism: Ordered domains locally increase magnetocrystalline anisotropy and serve as domain-wall pinning sites, elevating coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in coercive field in the Al-doped, partially B2-ordered sample compared to the Al-free reference under identical processing conditions.
generation.baseline: An equivalent CoFeMnNi-based alloy without Al doping subjected to the same melting and annealing schedule.
generation.boundary: Elevated Al content (>5 at.%) or incomplete ordering due to insufficient annealing may diminish the effect on coercivity.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al content, annealing parameters, and fraction of B2-phase required for maximal coercivity are not yet precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoFeMnNi-based HEAs: one with 5 at.% Al and one without Al. Arc-melt, homogenize, and anneal both sets identically at ~800 °C for 12–24 h. Compare their coercivity and B2-phase fraction via X-ray diffraction and magnetometry at room temperature.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Al-doped alloy fails to show partial B2 ordering or does not exhibit an increased coercive field relative to the undoped baseline.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

chosen.lever: Al addition in CoFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy
chosen.technique: Arc melting of CoFeMnNi(Al)x with subsequent vacuum annealing
chosen.conditions: Hold at ~800–900 °C for 12–24 hours and then cool to room temperature for magnetic characterization
chosen.why: Testable hypothesis: Adding ~5 at.% Al to a CoFeMnNi high-entropy alloy and annealing to induce partial B2-phase ordering will increase domain-wall pinning and boost magnetocrystalline anisotropy, thereby raising the coercive field. Compared to an Al-free baseline, the expected outcome is a measurable increase in coercivity at room temperature. Prior studies on Al-doped HEAs indicate that B2-type ordering phases contribute to enhanced magnetic hardness. An experimental falsification would involve systematically preparing both doped and undoped specimens under identical conditions and measuring minimal or no difference in coercivity, contradicting the hypothesized effect of Al-induced domain-wall pinning on coercivity.
